q2.answer: In the bone of the gum (upper jaw), next to the front teeth. It is called the alveolar cleft.
q2.where: Sheet 1, key message box and 'What this model shows'

q3.answer: The small tooth next to the front tooth (lateral incisor) never grew, which is called agenesis. About half of children with a cleft do not have this tooth on the cleft side.

q4.answer: The eye tooth needs bone to grow into and come down into. Without bone in the gap it would have nothing to move through.
q4.where: Sheet 1, 'The eye tooth' and 'Why surgeons do the bone graft'

q5.answer: At about 8 to 11 years old, picked by how far the teeth have grown rather than by age. The best time is before the eye tooth comes through the gum.

q6.answer: Most often from the hip. It is soft, spongy bone.

q7.answer: New bone fills the gap and the gum has healed over it. The graft joins the two parts of the upper jaw. The eye tooth is a little lower than before.
q7.where: Sheet 2, key message box and 'What has changed'

q8.answer: With an X-ray at about 3 to 6 months after surgery, which shows how well the new bone has taken.

q9.answer: Your hip can be sore for a while after the bone is taken. In one study children went back to school after about 2 weeks.

q10.answer: It has come down through the new bone and is fully in the row of teeth. If it gets stuck, a small operation uncovers it and braces pull it down.

q11.answer: Fixed braces. Almost everyone who has this graft needs them.

q12.answer: Two main plans. Close the space: braces move the eye tooth into the gap, then the dentist reshapes it and adds tooth-coloured filling (used most often). Keep the space: while still growing, a removable plate with a false tooth; after growth stops, the gap can be filled for good with an implant (post with a crown) or a bridge (false tooth with one wing glued behind the next tooth). The cleft team will talk it through with you.
